# The Recall ## Overview ### Key Elements - **Key Passage** - Review - **Scripture Memory** - "Carry one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ." Galatians 6:2 - **Catechism** - Q: How are Christians to relate to one another? A: Community. ## Conclusion > For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them. << Matthew 18:20 > Woe to him that is alone. David was alone when, Satan drew him to defile his neighbor's wife. While the sheep flock together they are safe, as being under the shepherd's eye; but if one straggle from the rest, it is quickly a prey to the ravenous wolf. It is no hard matter to rob that house that stands far from neighbors. The cruel pirate Satan watches for those vessels that sail without a convoy. << George Swinnock, _The Christian Man's Calling_ In this study, we coursed through biblical waters to discover God's plan for Christian community. Knowing that God is himself is a community—God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—we would expect no less than interpersonal relationships being a vital component of our Christian faith. In fact, the path toward Christian maturity involves growth in the way we interact with others. The Scriptures instruct disciples how to faithfully relate to others in various spheres of life. It is this simple and important agenda that has occupied the sessions of this book. The first six sessions of this book explored elements of Christian community that grow out of an ordered family. In Genesis 15:1–19:38, we saw the foundational and formative importance of the family in shaping all other interpersonal relationships. The narrative about Isaac and Rebekah in Genesis 24:1–67 provided a meaningful portrait of marriage: a sacred union of one man and one woman joined together in covenant relationship. Within the context of a godly marriage, parents raise their children to follow God's ways. In 1 Samuel 1:1–3:21 we recounted principles of parenting from Hannah and Samuel (and the contrast of Eli and his sons). The deep bond of friendship between David and Jonathan in 1 Samuel 18:1–20:42 provided an inspiring vision for genuine friendship and fraternal camaraderie. In Daniel 1:1–2:49 and 4:1–6:28, we observed Daniel navigate meaningful engagement in the public sector in a way that was faithful to God's ways. Then, we witnessed Nehemiah embrace his vocation (and lifework) in Nehemiah 1:1–7:4 in such a way that is instructive for disciples of all cultures and epochs. God builds his people—the community of faith—as an ordered household. In Mark 3:7–35, we saw Jesus build his church as a family of faithful Christ followers. Heeding Jesus' teaching in Matthew 17:22–18:35, we learned about essential community virtues that bind God's people together in genuine care and selfless service. Christian community is enjoyed with such a depth that members steward (and even sell) their possessions to meet urgent needs within the community of faith, as we saw in Acts 4:32–6:7. Christians need to learn how to relate to leaders and other churches. The narrative of Acts 14:19–16:5 helped guide us toward this end. Placed in a hostile world of competing values, Christians need to learn to winsomely and wisely engage various domains of society. A brief glimpse at Paul's second missionary journey in Acts 16:6–18:17 helped facilitate this exploration. Finally, Paul's circuitous journey to Rome in Acts 27:1–28:31 helped to instruct us how Christians should engage those who are outsiders. This study does not cover everything that can (and should) be said about Christian community. It does, however, offer an introductory and formative exposure to this most important topic of the Christian faith. The narratives are as instructional as they are inspiring. We simply cannot mature in our faith without attending to the domain of interpersonal relationships. As we grow in these various spheres—and strengthen the bond between us—we progress as disciples of Christ. Such progress leads us one step further toward the rich joys and blessings promised for followers of Jesus. In this final session, use the following pages as a means to review, synthesize, commit, and celebrate all that God has done in your midst! ## Book Overview: Surveying the Landscape ### Key Idea ### Story Retell ### Narrative Review ## Faith Foundation: Exploring the Terrain ### Discussion Questions ### Significant Insights ## Learning Plan: Charting the Course ### Selected Passages | Session | Topic | Passages | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Session 1 | Family | Genesis 2:4–25; Christine D. Pohl, _Making Room_ | ## Core Project: Synthesizing the Faith ### Community Covenant God calls us into covenant relationships with himself and other believers. As a community or as an individual, write a **community covenant** that serves as a condensed, memorable summary of the core biblical teachings on Christian community (consider a line, phrase, or short sentence for each topic/session in this study). The **community covenant** should be **short** (summarizes the key biblical teachings in a condensed and accessible format), **memorable** (articulates biblical principles in a way that is easily memorizable), **usable** (expresses the covenant as a statement that can be affirmed and confessed together as a church community), **accurate** (makes correct, biblical affirmations of Christian community), and **comprehensive** (addresses all major domains of interpersonal relationships). ### Journal Reflection ## Faith Practice: Following the Way ### Growth Evaluation | Objective |
